title: Crafted Villages
intro: This chapter chronicles the journey of Le Pham Khanh Chi, a 12th-grade student at the Foreign Language Specialized School, as she transforms her passion for chemistry and cultural heritage into a lifelong commitment to Vietnam's craft villages. Her work rests on three pillars, science that treats their waters, a heart that listens to people first, and a love for the heritage they carry.

blocks.text: Solar-Powered Craft Village Water Treatment Boat

row.alt: Khánh Chi hàn mạch điện tử trên bàn thí nghiệm
row.note: I set out to build a solar-powered water-treatment boat from recycled materials – a fusion of sunlight, sensors, and chemistry, designed to help craft villages see and treat their water.

row.alt: Mô hình thuyền xử lí nước có tấm pin mặt trời, bên cạnh bo mạch điều khiển
row.note: After months in the lab, the design came together: an ESP32 reading pH, TDS, temperature; a paddle wheel to aerate the water; a swappable adsorbent module – HAp/PANI for dyes, rice-husk activated carbon for heavy metals; and a hull built to glide past the weeds and debris in water.

row.alt: Tay đặt thuyền năng lượng mặt trời xuống mặt nước kênh
row.note: With its swappable adsorbent module, it is now not only a proof of concept but a floating treatment system, ready to make an impact on the water of craft villages and the heritage that depends on it.

row.alt: Khánh Chi ngồi xổm bên bờ kênh, chuẩn bị thả thuyền xuống nước
row.note: It was finally time to take my creation to the village’s edge. Seeing it in action on real water made all the experiments worth it.

blocks.text: About 170 kilometers west of Hanoi lies Pa Co, home of the H'Mong people, where brocade glows in every color. Behind it, the ditches run with the dye that colored it. I wondered where that color goes. Under the Kaleidoscope of the Past Project, I came with chemistry, love for this culture, and compassion for its waters to promote its colors while preserving its rivers.

row.alt: Khánh Chi cúi xuống thả thiết bị đo bên ao, phụ nữ H'Mong đứng xem
Khánh Chi cầm bộ điều khiển, chiếc thuyền nhỏ chạy trên mặt ao

blocks.text: Industrial dye had become a habit in Pa Co, and its leftovers a quiet burden on the canals beside the families’ homes. Here, I introduced the locals to my Solar-Powered Water Treatment Boat – the way sunlight powers it, how HAp/PANI draws the dye out of the water, and how to read its sensors.

video.alt: Video: phỏng vấn bác Việt, trưởng thôn, về vấn đề nước thải

blocks.text: An interview with Mr. Sung A Viet, head of Cha Day village in Pa Co, on the wastewater that flows through the village's canals.

video.alt: Video: phỏng vấn người dân về thói quen sinh hoạt, xử lí nước thải

blocks.text: An interview with families in Pa Co about their daily routines, and where the water goes when the dyeing is done.

video.alt: Video: giới thiệu với người dân làng Pà Cò về thuyền xử lí nước thải nhuộm

blocks.text: Introducing the people of Pa Co to a boat that treats dye wastewater, with the adsorbent built right into it.

row.alt: Khánh Chi cùng một phụ nữ H'Mong đeo gùi hái lá trong rừng
Khánh Chi ngồi cùng người dân chặt rễ cây lấy màu nhuộm
Khánh Chi cho lá cây vào thùng nước để ngâm lấy màu

blocks.text: Cleaning the water was only half the solution; what’s there to dye instead of industrial bright colors? I followed the locals into the forest, finding roots, leaves, and bark that hold color. Back in the courtyard, I helped them dye the fibre thread, shade after shade, brighter than I had ever imagined. By evening, the gaps between my fingers were full of the color of those roots.

row.alt: Khánh Chi cầm tấm vải chàm vẽ sáp, phía sau là dãy vải nhuộm nhiều màu phơi trên dây

row.text: After long days of chopping forest roots, boiling, steeping, and testing, the colors came out lovelier than I had dared to hope. And every shade, from the reds to the blues, came from plants alone.

blocks.text: Gallery: Patterns of the H'Mong

marquee.alt: Những tấm vải H'Mong vẽ sáp, nhuộm chàm và nâu, treo cạnh nhau
marquee.note: This gallery features patterns of the H'Mong, all made by hand. The fabric is woven from flax fiber, and each pattern is drawn in beeswax, which keeps the cloth its white color wherever it is painted before dyeing.

marquee.alt: Cận cảnh vải nâu với hoa văn sừng cừu đan vào nhau
marquee.note: This brown cloth is dyed from dye yam (Dioscorea cirrhosa), a forest tuber. Its main motif, interlocking ram's horns, stands for couples and the love between partners in H'Mong villages.

marquee.alt: Tấm vải chàm vẽ sáp hình cô gái H'Mong đeo vòng cổ
marquee.note: Drawn in beeswax on a field of blue, featuring a H'Mong girl. The color comes from Assam indigo leaves (Strobilanthes cusia), simmered and left to steep for several days.

marquee.alt: Vải xanh chàm đậm với hoa văn tròn hình măng đắng, viền đỏ
marquee.note: This features the bitter bamboo shoot, a common plant of Pa Co's forest. The deep navy blue comes from the same Assam indigo leaves, steeped for longer to reach this deep shade.

marquee.alt: Vải chàm với hoa văn mặt trời, tâm màu đỏ
marquee.note: At the very center is the red sun, a symbol of hope and of a village that flourishes. The red at its heart comes from gac fruit (Momordica cochinchinensis).

marquee.alt: Khánh Chi cùng anh Huy đứng giữa các bộ trang phục cổ may từ vải nhuộm tự nhiên
marquee.note: Returning to the city, I met Mr. Huy, founder of Dong Phong Atelier to promote traditional Vietnamese attire of earlier centuries, made from Pa Co's naturally dyed cloth.

blocks.text: Gallery: Traditional Attire in Natural Color

These vibrant colors are all extracted from natural plants. Purple is magenta plant (Peristrophe roxburghiana). Green blends Assam indigo (Strobilanthes cusia) with yellow vine (Fibraurea recisa). Yellow comes from turmeric (Curcuma longa), and deep brown from dye yam (Dioscorea cirrhosa).

row.alt: Hai bộ áo cổ màu tím và xanh lá trên giá treo, phía trên là nón lá
Hai bộ áo cổ màu vàng nghệ và nâu hoa văn trên giá treo
Hai bộ áo cổ màu xanh rêu và nâu cam trên giá treo

video.alt: Video: buổi workshop Morning Tea, Traditional Costume, and Calligraphy

row.alt: Ảnh tập thể người tham dự workshop, nhiều người mặc cổ phục
Diễn giả cầm micro nói chuyện, bên cạnh là các bạn mặc cổ phục
Khánh Chi và bạn mặc áo cổ phục đỏ, xanh, cầm micro giới thiệu

blocks.text: To bring these costumes out of the studio and in front of people, I co-organized Morning Tea, Traditional Costume, and Calligraphy, a workshop to display them and introduce audiences to clothing made from natural color.

I guided guests through how Vietnamese attire changed across the centuries, with illustrations we drew ourselves. Then Mr. Dong, author of "Weaving a Dynasty," joined us at my invitation to share his knowledge of historical costume culture.

Less than an hour south of Hanoi, beside the Red River, lies Thuong Tin, my mother's hometown, and inside it two small craft villages: Ha Thai, where artisans paint lacquer, and Ninh So, where hands weave bamboo and rattan. These lanes have always felt like home. This time I came back with chemistry and a question – what does the river carry away from the places I love?

row.alt: Thuyền năng lượng mặt trời nổi giữa mặt nước đục, nhiều rác
Khánh Chi ngồi xổm bên bờ kênh, đeo găng tay chỉnh thuyền
Khánh Chi đứng trên bờ cầm bộ điều khiển thuyền

blocks.text: Again, I zoom into the water. It is hard to believe that the lacquer paintings and woven baskets on the shelves come from the same place as this river, and the sight gave me goosebumps. So I brought my solar-powered boat onto it, loaded with rice-husk activated carbon, to draw out what the craft leaves behind.
1. Ha Thai Lacquer Village

row.alt: Khánh Chi chụp ảnh các tranh sơn mài trên kệ trưng bày
Khánh Chi giơ máy ảnh chụp các tượng sơn mài

blocks.text: I co-organized an exhibition-sale for the village's artisans and was responsible for its reach to the mass, and my part was to carry the pieces out of the studio and into people's feeds through photographing their pieces and sharing them online.

video.alt: Video: phỏng vấn nghệ nhân về quy trình và vấn đề ô nhiễm nước ở làng nghề Hạ Thái

blocks.text: Interview with an artisan about the sanding and silver-leafing process and the village's water pollution.
Above all, let my gallery guide you through the works.
Gallery: Layers of Light (featuring lacquer handmade crafts)

marquee.alt: Những hộp sơn mài đen vẽ mặt người kiểu lập thể, xếp trên kệ kính
marquee.note: What happens when a traditional craft meets modern art? These boxes are almost Cubist faces and one gold-toned design that echoes Klimt, each lid a small canvas on a glossy black ground.

marquee.alt: Tranh sơn mài thiếu nữ áo dài đội nón lá trên nền đen
marquee.note: Women in áo dài, their faces tucked beneath pale conical hats, each dressed in her own soft palette – teal and white, pink and violet, orange and blue. Set against a deep black ground, the gowns glow by contrast, an old lacquer trick of letting darkness bring color forward.

marquee.alt: Tranh sơn mài Chùa Một Cột trong khung đen bóng
marquee.note: Hanoi's cultural heritage, painted in lacquer: one of the works that capture the city's landmarks, this one featuring the One Pillar Pagoda.

marquee.alt: Tượng sơn mài thiếu nữ đội nón lá nhiều màu cam, trắng, xanh
marquee.note: Orange, white, blue, green, yellow: women in ao dai and conical hats, reduced to a few clean lines. Each carries a tiny painted scene on its body, and pieces in colors like these are traditionally finished with silver applied by hand.

marquee.alt: Hai con rối nước sơn trắng rạn, môi đỏ, đeo vòng bạc ở cổ
marquee.note: These figures remind of the humor in Vietnamese water puppets in painted brows, red lips, a silver ring at the neck, and a crackled white surface that gives them the patina of age.

blocks.text: 2. Ninh So Bamboo and Rattan Weaving Village

Under the same large village Thuong Tin, where there are no glossy colors of lacquer, Ninh So feels quieter. Here the palette is the plain gold of bamboo and rattan, and most of the hands that weave it are older ones.

video.alt: Video: trò chuyện cùng nghệ nhân làng Ninh Sở, tìm hiểu cách làm và mặt hàng

blocks.text: I had a conversation with Mrs. Hoai about how bamboo and rattan pieces are made, and the range of goods the village weaves.

row.alt: Nghệ nhân đan sọt tre trước hiên nhà, Khánh Chi ngồi chụp ảnh
Xưởng đan với nhiều sọt tre, người thợ ngồi làm giữa đống hàng

blocks.text: Again, I photographed the artisans' pieces and promoted them on mass media, so the beauty of a plain-colored craft could reach people who had never seen it up close.

row.alt: Khánh Chi đội nón ngồi giữa gian hàng mây tre đan tại hội chợ
Khánh Chi đứng trước phông Lễ hội Sản phẩm Xanh 2026

blocks.text: I registered a booth for Ninh So’s weavers at the Green Agriculture Festival, to bring their bamboo and rattan work to new buyers and move the craft toward a more valued business.

About 100 kilometers from Hanoi, in Nam Dinh Province, lies Xoi Tri, a village that has blown glass by hand for around seventy years. Its beer glasses, a fixture of Hanoi's street corners, have always been made from shards of old glass. It was the right place for Eco-Wander, my project about giving used glass a second life.

video.alt: Video: Khánh Chi phân loại chai thuỷ tinh tại làng Xôi Trì

row.alt: Khánh Chi xếp chai thuỷ tinh vào két nhựa bên đường làng

blocks.text: I collected used glass from households across the village, bottle by bottle, sorting each as I went. In a village that has blown glass for generations, nearly every home held a little of its own raw material.

row.alt: Khánh Chi đeo găng tay phân loại chai thuỷ tinh nhiều màu
Khánh Chi đeo găng tay bóc nhãn một chai thuỷ tinh
Tay cọ rửa chai thuỷ tinh trong thùng nước

blocks.text: I sorted bottles by color and label, stripped caps and plastic wrap, and soaked and scrubbed off stubborn labels, before crushing the glass into small pieces.

row.alt: Tay gắn mảnh thuỷ tinh vụn lên tranh vẽ trong khung gỗ
Hai bạn học sinh vẽ tranh tại bàn workshop
Các tranh kính tái chế và lọ màu acrylic trên bàn workshop

blocks.text: Under the Eco-Wander project, I organized a workshop on the theme of Vietnamese tradition, where recycled glass was decorated and glazed, taking on a glossy, vivid finish that catches the eye.

row.alt: Khách xem các bức tranh kính tái chế xếp dọc bàn triển lãm
Standee triển lãm Việt Nam Gấm Hoa bên cạnh thú bông
Dãy tranh kính tái chế trưng bày trên bàn phủ khăn đen

blocks.text: What began as bottles thrown away ended as art on canvas. At the Viet Nam Brocade and Blossoms exhibition, which I organized, recycled glass artworks were shown and sold to support the Vietnam Cerebral Palsy Association.

Gallery: Vietnam in Splendor
(featuring a few of the exhibition's recycled glass paintings)

marquee.alt: Tranh kính tái chế: con thuyền giữa vách đá vôi trên mặt nước xanh ngọc
marquee.note: Among the Cliffs, a lone boat drifts toward limestone cliffs on emerald water. The green of the water comes from crushed beer bottles.

marquee.alt: Tranh kính tái chế: thiếu nữ áo đỏ cầm hoa trên nền lá xanh
marquee.note: Blossom's Grace features a woman in vivid red holds a blossom against lush green. Her deep red-brown blossom comes from wine bottles, and the clear glass around her from water and soft-drink bottles.

marquee.alt: Tranh kính tái chế: thuyền chở hoa sen hồng giữa nước xanh và lá sen
marquee.note: Lotus Drift, a boat loaded with pink blossoms drifts through teal water and green leaves. The flowers began as perfume bottles, the leaves as beer bottles, the shadows at the edges as wine bottles.

marquee.alt: Tranh kính tái chế: người nông dân đội nón gặt lúa chín vàng
marquee.note: Golden Season features farmers in conical hats harvest a vast field of ripe rice under a soft sky. The gold of the rice comes from cosmetic serum glass bottles.

marquee.alt: Tranh kính tái chế: cốm xanh gói lá sen bên hoa sen
marquee.note: Fragrance of Green Rice, young green rice wrapped in lotus leaves beside blooming lotus. The pale greens come from soda and soju bottles.

marquee.alt: Tranh kính tái chế: ánh nắng rọi vào hang Sơn Đoòng, người chèo thuyền kayak trên nước xanh
marquee.note: Son Doong Cave, sunbeams pour through the cave opening onto turquoise water, where a lone kayaker drifts. The dark rim is wine bottles and the glints along the water are clear water bottles.
